A decade after the Brexit vote, the UK and EU are set to start resetting relations (File: AP)By Al Jazeera Staff and AFPPublished On 20 Nov 202620 Nov 2026
British and European Union leaders are set to meet at a summit billed as a chance to reset relations a decade after the Brexit vote.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa, who heads the European Council, on Friday in Brussels. In the second such meeting since Britain formally left the bloc in 2020, deals on food, emissions and youth mobility are expected to be sealed.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Far from Trump-Putin meeting, Europe to count cost of Ukraine’s defencelist 2 of 3Andy Burnham says Brexit is what the UK’s ‘enemies’ wantedlist 3 of 3Britain’s Brexit woes: ‘I didn’t vote to leave in the way that we did’end of list
The previous summit in 2025 was billed as a “stable foundation” upon which to rebuild the relationship between London and Brussels. Friday’s meeting is being sold as a chance to start on a reset of relations.
Burnham said earlier in the week that it was an “obvious truth” that Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit, which followed a non-binding referendum in 2016 in which 52 percent of the British public voted to leave the EU. He has signalled that a reformed relationship with Brussels is on his agenda.
The most valuable agreement on the table concerns the cross-border exchange of animals, plants and related products. Britain has estimated that the removal of the current controls could be worth 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7bn) annually.

Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruling over whether Myanmar committed genocide against their people, on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar, on November 19, 2026 [AFP]By Masum BillahPublished On 20 Nov 202620 Nov 2026
Dhaka, Bangladesh — Umme Ruman was watching the news on her mobile phone from her shelter in Camp 1E of the Rohingya refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. She had been waiting for the International Court of Justice (ICJ) verdict since the afternoon. But poor internet connectivity kept interrupting the live broadcast.
Then she opened Facebook and saw a headline: “ICJ confirms Myanmar committed genocide.”
Overwhelmed, she jumped. Her sister-in-law was cooking. Ruman rushed to hug her. Before she could explain what had happened, she broke down in tears.
“I celebrated with tears of joy because, for the first time, the world acknowledged what happened to us,” she said.
On Thursday, the ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya during brutal military operations in 2017, in which the court found more than 10,000 people had been killed.
The landmark judgement in the case, brought before the court by The Gambia, recognised the atrocities committed against the community after years of denial. For refugees who have spent nearly a decade waiting for justice, the ruling brought a wave of relief, emotion and renewed hope.
“For me, this is not simply a legal verdict. It is proof of our suffering,” Ruman said.
Across the camps, people followed the announcement on mobile phones, laptops and large screens. Some watched with friends. Others gathered with their families. Many turned to Facebook and YouTube to follow the proceedings.

In the Sabra neighbourhood in southern Gaza City, the vehicle the Civil Defence team was using broke down while the crew was responding to an Israeli air strike on the area [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/Al Jazeera]By Maram HumaidPublished On 20 Nov 202620 Nov 2026
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – Palestinian Civil Defence crews heard an explosion nearby and rushed to respond. But instead of taking a fire engine – the only vehicle available to the team at the time – they had to grab their equipment and rush to help on foot. The fire engine wasn’t working.
“We heard the strike, opened the vehicle, took our equipment and ran,” said Abdullah al-Majdalawi, a Civil Defence field officer, describing the response to an Israeli attack near the al-Qattan Centre on November 3. It took about 10 minutes for the crew to reach the site, carrying their equipment, and then carrying injured people back. They also recovered the body of someone killed in the strike.

In a separate incident in southern Gaza City’s Sabra neighbourhood last month, the vehicle the Civil Defence team was using broke down while the crew was responding to an Israeli air strike on the area.

A man walks in front of a mural symbolising restrictions on shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's key shipping lanes, in Sanaa, Yemen, Monday, September 14, 2026 [Osamah Abdulrahman/AP Photo]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 20 Nov 202620 Nov 2026
Sanaa, Yemen – Yazan, 28, filled up his car at a petrol station in Sanaa and began a trip towards the city of Ibb to the south.
The journey would usually take about two and a half hours, but as he accelerated along the road, Yazan noticed that the car was struggling to pick up speed.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Yemen’s besieged city of Taiz faces a deepening water crisislist 2 of 3Saudi Arabia says Houthi attack damaged Riyadh towerlist 3 of 3Saudi coalition hits 60 Houthi military sites; Taiz sees ‘fierce battles’end of list
Yazan, who did not want to give his full name, explained that the harder he pressed the accelerator, the more the engine vibrated. The unusual engine noise and vibration forced him to stop several times on the road.
It eventually took Yazan six hours to reach his destination. He believes the problem was caused by contaminated petrol – fuel mixed with oil and impurities – that he bought in Sanaa.
“The petrol left numerous cars, including mine, with many faults,” Yazan told Al Jazeera. “We pay for the expensive petrol that damages our engines.”
Yazan is not alone. Other drivers in Sanaa have reported similar problems with contaminated and increasingly expensive petrol.
The cause of the issue is disputed. In June, the Sanaa-based Yemen Petroleum Company (YPC), run by the Houthis who have controlled northwest Yemen since 2014, said contaminated fuel was the result of inadequately equipped fuel storage facilities in Hodeidah.
